segments.narration: His will promised a fortune to Toronto's biggest family. Charles Vance Millar, a lawyer, financier and career prankster, died in 1926 and left the city a puzzle.
The clause was exact. Whichever Toronto mother had the most children in the ten years after his death would take the residue of his estate.
The same will handed brewery shares to teetotal ministers and racetrack stock to men who campaigned against racing. Millar was not being careless.
Relatives and the province fought for years to void it. In 1938 the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the clause and let the thing stand.
Four Toronto mothers, nine children each, split it: about a hundred and ten thousand dollars apiece. The joke outlasted every lawyer sent to kill it.
